title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: Quality control (QC) critical first step single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. goal QC identify remove low-quality cells confound downstream analysis. Poor quality cells can arise several sources: empty droplets contain ambient RNA, dying cells compromised membranes. module, work single nuclei RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) data human heart tissue. data comes study examining human heart development across three stages: foetal, young, adult (Sim et al., 2021, Circulation). Understanding heart changes cellular level across development provides insights cardiac maturation potential therapeutic targets.

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: Traditional “bulk” RNA-sequencing measures average gene expression across millions cells. powerful, approach masks heterogeneity exists within tissues. Single cell RNA-sequencing overcomes limitation measuring gene expression individual cells, allowing us : Identify distinct cell types within tissue Discover rare cell populations Study cell--cell variability Track cellular states development disease widely used platform scRNA-seq 10X Genomics Chromium system, captures cells oil droplets along barcoded beads. bead carries oligonucleotides three key components: Cell barcode: Identifies cell RNA came Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI): Identifies individual RNA molecules, removing PCR amplification bias Poly-dT tail: Captures polyadenylated mRNA

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: Now calculate key QC metrics cell. Seurat provides PercentageFeatureSet() function calculate percentage counts specified set genes. Let us understand metrics tell us: nCount_RNA (library size): total number UMI counts cell. low values suggest empty droplets; high values may indicate technical artefacts. nFeature_RNA (gene count): number genes detected. Correlates library size provides additional information transcriptome complexity. percent.mt: Percentage counts mitochondrial genes. High values (typically >10-20%) suggest dying cells. percent.ribo: Percentage counts ribosomal genes. Varies cell type; highly proliferative cells often higher ribosomal content.
code: # Calculate the percentage of counts from mitochondrial genes # pattern = "^MT-" matches gene names starting with "MT-" seu[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(seu, pattern = "^MT-")  # Calculate the percentage of counts from ribosomal genes seu[["percent.ribo"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(seu, pattern = "^RP[SL]")  # View summary statistics for all QC metrics summary(seu@meta.data[, c("nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA", "percent.mt", "percent.ribo")]) ##    nCount_RNA      nFeature_RNA     percent.mt       percent.ribo     ##  Min.   :   500   Min.   :  212   Min.   : 0.0000   Min.   : 0.0000   ##  1st Qu.:  5932   1st Qu.: 2650   1st Qu.: 0.1032   1st Qu.: 0.3511   ##  Median :  9365   Median : 3358   Median : 0.2522   Median : 0.5275   ##  Mean   : 10686   Mean   : 3293   Mean   : 1.5203   Mean   : 0.8745   ##  3rd Qu.: 13370   3rd Qu.: 3997   3rd Qu.: 1.1316   3rd Qu.: 0.8531   ##  Max.   :251820   Max.   :15259   Max.   :83.0145   Max.   :19.3012

title: Module 1: Quality Control

title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: remove four categories genes, specific reasons: 1. Nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes (~200 genes) genes nuclear genome encode proteins functioning within mitochondria (e.g., mitochondrial ribosomal proteins like MRPL20, MRPS15). expression correlates cellular metabolic state can confound biological comparisons. Note MT-prefixed genes (encoded mitochondrial genome ) already excluded data preprocessing. 2. Ribosomal protein genes (~190 genes) Ribosomal proteins (RPS RPL gene families) highly ubiquitously expressed across cell types. dominate variance calculations without providing useful biological insight distinguishing developmental disease-related transcriptional changes. 3. Genes without Entrez IDs (~9,000 genes) Genes lacking Entrez identifiers often pseudogenes, non-coding transcripts, poorly characterised sequences. Removing simplifies downstream functional annotation pathway analysis, Entrez IDs commonly required. 4. Sex chromosome genes (~800 genes) unbalanced sex distribution across developmental groups dataset (fetal: 2M/1F, young: 2M/1F, adult: 1M/2F), X Y chromosome genes may show spurious differential expression driven sample composition rather true developmental biology. Removing prevents confounding.

text: quality control, dataset high-quality cells. However, can identify cell types, must address two important challenges: Technical variation: Raw count data affected differences sequencing depth cells. cell total counts appear higher expression genes, even underlying biology identical. Normalisation removes technical variation. Batch effects: Cells processed different batches (different days, different samples) may show systematic differences unrelated biology. Integration methods correct batch effects preserving true biological variation. module, normalise data using SCTransform, integrate samples using Harmony, identify cell clusters using graph-based clustering. overall workflow follows standard single cell analysis pipeline: step builds upon previous one, progressively transforming data raw gene counts biologically interpretable cell clusters.

SCTransform (Hafemeister & Satija, 2019) uses regularised negative binomial regression normalise UMI count data. approach: Models relationship observed counts sequencing depth gene using negative binomial distribution Computes Pearson residuals represent deviation expected expression given sequencing depth Identifies genes high biological variability (variable features) drive downstream analyses key insight highly expressed genes show variance simply due sampling effects. SCTransform accounts modelling mean-variance relationship, allowing fair comparison across genes different expression levels. vst.flavor = "v2" option uses improved algorithm (Choudhary & Satija, 2022) : Uses geometric mean library size reference (robust) Implements improved regularisation better handling outliers Provides stable results large datasets SCTransform automatically identifies highly variable genes. Let us examine top variable features: can visualise mean-variance relationship:

text: analysing data multiple samples batches, cells often cluster sample origin rather cell type. happens sample unique technical characteristics (slight differences dissociation, library preparation, sequencing) create systematic biases. Harmony (Korsunsky et al., 2019) fast effective integration method corrects batch effects preserving biological variation. algorithm works follows: Soft clustering: Cells assigned probabilistically multiple clusters PCA space Calculate centroids: cluster, compute centroid separately batch Adjust embeddings: Move cells toward global centroid, removing batch-specific shifts Iterate: Repeat convergence key advantage Harmony operates directly PCA embeddings, making fast memory-efficient. Unlike methods require re-analysis raw counts, Harmony can integrate datasets seconds minutes. Epicardial         "UPK3B", "WT1",         # Proliferating         "MKI67", "TOP2A"     ),     celltype = c(         rep("Cardiomyocytes", 9),         rep("Fibroblasts", 7),         rep("Pericytes", 4),         rep("Endothelial", 5),         rep("Smooth Muscle", 4),         rep("Macrophages", 5),         rep("T Cells", 4),         rep("Schwann", 3),         rep("Epicardial", 2),         rep("Proliferating", 2)     ) )  # Define colors for each cell type celltype_colors <- c(     "Cardiomyocytes" = "#D62728",     "Fibroblasts" = "#1F77B4",     "Pericytes" = "#2CA02C",     "Endothelial" = "#9467BD",     "Smooth Muscle" = "#FF7F0E",     "Macrophages" = "#8C564B",     "T Cells" = "#E377C2",     "Schwann" = "#7F7F7F",     "Epicardial" = "#17BECF",     "Proliferating" = "#333333" )  # Filter to available genes marker_info <- marker_info[marker_info$gene %in% rownames(seu), ] marker_genes <- marker_info$gene gene_colors <- celltype_colors[marker_info$celltype] marker_info$celltype_f <- factor(marker_info$celltype, levels = names(celltype_colors))  # Order clusters by cell type identity for diagonal pattern # Preferred order: CMs first (fetal, mature, atrial), then stromal, immune, neural preferred_order <- c("0", "7", "10", "14", "9", "2", "4", "8", "13", "1", "3", "15", "5", "11", "6", "16", "12") # Filter to only clusters that exist in our data actual_clusters <- as.character(unique(seu$seurat_clusters)) cluster_order <- preferred_order[preferred_order %in% actual_clusters] # Add any clusters not in preferred order (shouldn't happen, but safety) cluster_order <- c(cluster_order, setdiff(actual_clusters, cluster_order)) seu$cluster_ordered <- factor(seu$seurat_clusters, levels = cluster_order)  # Calculate cell type label positions celltype_positions <- marker_info %>%     mutate(pos = row_number()) %>%     group_by(celltype_f) %>%     summarise(start = min(pos) - 0.5, end = max(pos) + 0.5,               mid = mean(pos), .groups = "drop")  # Create DotPlot with cell type annotations DotPlot(seu, features = marker_genes, group.by = "cluster_ordered") +     RotatedAxis() +     scale_colour_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",                            midpoint = 0, name = "Average\nExpression") +     scale_size_continuous(name = "Percent\nExpressed", range = c(0.5, 6)) +     labs(x = NULL, y = "Cluster",          title = "Cell Type Marker Expression (Sim et al. 2021)") +     theme_bw() +     theme(         plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),         axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 10,                                    color = gene_colors, face = "italic"),         axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12),         axis.title.y = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),         panel.grid.major = element_blank(),         panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),         panel.border = element_rect(color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.8),         legend.position = "right",         legend.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),         legend.text = element_text(size = 10),         plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 45, 10)     ) +     # Add cell type color bars     annotate("rect",              xmin = celltype_positions$start, xmax = celltype_positions$end,              ymin = -1.8, ymax = -1.2,              fill = celltype_colors[as.character(celltype_positions$celltype_f)]) +     # Add cell type labels inside bars     annotate("text",              x = celltype_positions$mid, y = -1.5,              label = celltype_positions$celltype_f,              size = 3.5, angle = 0, hjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold",              color = "white") +     coord_cartesian(clip = "off", ylim = c(0.5, length(cluster_order) + 0.5))

title: Module 4: Differential Expression Analysis
text: critical pitfall single cell differential expression analysis pseudoreplication: treating cells independent biological replicates . Cells sample share technical biological variation violates independence assumption statistical tests. Consider analogy: want compare heights two populations, measuring person multiple times increase sample size. Similarly, capturing 5,000 cells one individual give us 5,000 independent observations individual’s biology. Many single cell DE methods (Wilcoxon test, t-test, MAST) operate cell level treat cell independent replicate. approaches: Inflate Type error rates (false positives) dramatically Produce artificially small p-values reflect true significance Confound biological technical variation generalise findings beyond specific samples analysed solution pseudobulk analysis: aggregating counts across cells within sample create sample-level expression estimates, applying well-established bulk RNA-seq methods. approach: Correctly identifies biological replicate (sample/individual) Properly controls false discovery rates Accounts sample--sample variation Produces results generalise population

code: # Function to create contrasts for a cell type create_celltype_contrasts <- function(ct_short, design) {     # Get coefficient names containing this cell type     coefs <- colnames(design)     ct_coefs <- coefs[grep(paste0("^", ct_short, "\\."), coefs)]      if (length(ct_coefs) < 6) {         warning("Insufficient coefficients for ", ct_short)         return(NULL)     }      # Define contrasts averaging over sex     # Young vs Fetal     yvf <- paste0("0.5*(", ct_short, ".young.m + ", ct_short, ".young.f) - ",                   "0.5*(", ct_short, ".fetal.m + ", ct_short, ".fetal.f)")      # Adult vs Fetal     avf <- paste0("0.5*(", ct_short, ".adult.m + ", ct_short, ".adult.f) - ",                   "0.5*(", ct_short, ".fetal.m + ", ct_short, ".fetal.f)")      # Adult vs Young     avy <- paste0("0.5*(", ct_short, ".adult.m + ", ct_short, ".adult.f) - ",                   "0.5*(", ct_short, ".young.m + ", ct_short, ".young.f)")      # Use contrasts parameter (character vector) to avoid scoping issues     contrast_list <- c(yvf, avf, avy)     cm <- makeContrasts(contrasts = contrast_list, levels = design)     # Set proper column names for the contrast matrix     colnames(cm) <- c("YvF", "AvF", "AvY")     cm }

code: # Function to create volcano plot create_volcano <- function(fit_obj, coef_name, title) {     results <- topTreat(fit_obj, coef = coef_name, n = Inf)     results$significant <- results$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & abs(results$logFC) > 0.5      # Label top genes     top_genes <- results %>%         filter(significant) %>%         arrange(adj.P.Val) %>%         head(10)      ggplot(results, aes(x = logFC, y = -log10(adj.P.Val))) +         geom_point(aes(colour = significant), alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +         geom_text(             data = top_genes,             aes(label = SYMBOL),             size = 2.5, hjust = -0.1, vjust = 0.5,             check_overlap = TRUE         ) +         geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.5, 0.5), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +         geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +         scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey70", "TRUE" = "#D62728")) +         labs(             title = title,             x = "log2 Fold Change",             y = "-log10(adjusted P-value)"         ) +         theme_minimal() +         theme(legend.position = "none") }  # Create volcano plots for Adult vs Fetal across cell types v1 <- create_volcano(treat_cardio, "AvF", "Cardiomyocytes: Adult vs Fetal") v2 <- create_volcano(treat_fibro, "AvF", "Fibroblasts: Adult vs Fetal") v3 <- create_volcano(treat_endo, "AvF", "Endothelial: Adult vs Fetal") v4 <- create_volcano(treat_immune, "AvF", "Immune: Adult vs Fetal")  (v1 + v2) / (v3 + v4) +     plot_annotation(         title = "Volcano Plots: Adult vs Fetal Development",         subtitle = "Dashed lines indicate |logFC| > 0.5 and FDR < 0.05 thresholds"     )

code: # Get results for cardiomyocytes results_yvf <- topTreat(treat_cardio, coef = "YvF", n = Inf) results_avf <- topTreat(treat_cardio, coef = "AvF", n = Inf)  # Merge results trajectory_data <- data.frame(     gene = results_yvf$SYMBOL,     logFC_YvF = results_yvf$logFC,     logFC_AvF = results_avf$logFC[match(results_yvf$SYMBOL, results_avf$SYMBOL)],     sig_YvF = results_yvf$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & abs(results_yvf$logFC) > 0.5,     sig_AvF = results_avf$adj.P.Val < 0.05 & abs(results_avf$logFC) > 0.5 )  # Identify genes significant in either comparison trajectory_data$significant <- trajectory_data$sig_YvF | trajectory_data$sig_AvF  # Label genes significant in both trajectory_data$sig_both <- trajectory_data$sig_YvF & trajectory_data$sig_AvF label_genes <- trajectory_data %>%     filter(sig_both) %>%     arrange(desc(abs(logFC_AvF))) %>%     head(15)  ggplot(trajectory_data, aes(x = logFC_YvF, y = logFC_AvF)) +     geom_point(aes(colour = significant), alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +     geom_text(         data = label_genes,         aes(label = gene),         size = 2.5, colour = "black",         check_overlap = TRUE     ) +     geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +     geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +     geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +     scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey70", "TRUE" = "#D62728")) +     labs(         title = "Cardiomyocyte Developmental Trajectory",         subtitle = "Genes in upper-right/lower-left show progressive developmental changes",         x = "log2 FC: Young vs Fetal",         y = "log2 FC: Adult vs Fetal"     ) +     theme_minimal() +     theme(legend.position = "none") +     coord_fixed()

text: n=3 biological replicates per group, statistical power limited. several implications: Conservative estimates: may fail detect true biological effects (Type II errors) due insufficient power. Variance estimation: samples, variance estimates unstable. empirical Bayes moderation limma helps fully compensate. Outlier sensitivity: Individual outlier samples can outsized influence results. Effect size uncertainty: Confidence intervals log-fold-changes wide small samples.

text: Focus robust signals: Prioritise genes large effect sizes (|logFC| > 1) small p-values (FDR < 0.01). Seek consistency: Genes differentially expressed across multiple cell types showing progressive developmental changes likely represent true biological signals. Validate orthogonally: Important findings validated using independent methods (qPCR, protein staining) datasets. Consider biology: Interpret results context known cardiac developmental biology.

title: Module 4: Differential Expression Analysis
text: module, performed two complementary analyses human heart development: cell type composition analysis using propeller pseudobulk differential expression analysis using limma-voom pipeline. findings consistent reported Sim et al. (2021): Cell Type Composition (propeller analysis): human heart undergoes significant changes cellular composition development (FDR < 0.05 four major cell types) Cardiomyocyte proportions decrease dramatically ~73% (fetal) ~40% (young) ~22% (adult) Immune cell proportions increase ~3% (fetal) ~10% (young) ~18% (adult) Fibroblast proportions increase ~12% (fetal) ~28% (young) ~32% (adult) Endothelial cell proportions increase ~5% (fetal) ~10% (young) ~14% (adult) compositional changes reflect fundamental biological processes cardiac development, consistent original study findings Differential Expression (limma-voom analysis): pseudobulk approach correctly treats samples (cells) unit biological replication, avoiding pseudoreplication problem Cardiomyocytes show largest number differentially expressed genes (~2,200-2,300 genes Young vs Fetal Adult vs Fetal comparisons), consistent major functional maturation involving metabolic reprogramming cell cycle exit reported original study Fibroblasts show substantial transcriptional changes (~1,200-1,500 DE genes), reflecting expanding role extracellular matrix production Endothelial cells show ~570-700 DE genes immune cells ~320-420 DE genes, representing modest still biologically meaningful changes Interestingly, Adult vs Young comparison yields DE genes across cell types, suggesting developmental transcriptional changes occur fetal--postnatal transition rather later maturation Methodological Notes: limma-voom pipeline TREAT provides conservative reliable identification differentially expressed genes. Despite n=3 samples per group, successfully detected significant composition changes thousands differentially expressed genes, demonstrating even modest sample sizes can yield meaningful results biological signal strong. TREAT method (testing fold-changes exceeding threshold) ensures report genes biologically meaningful effect sizes, just statistically significant changes. additional biological insights including gene set enrichment sex-specific expression programmes, original study Sim et al. (2021) consulted.
